title: The Nature Of Free Will In The Age Of AI | NOEMA
gist: A compatibilist essay arguing that the Libet experiment and hard-determinist popularizations (Sapolsky, Harris) refute only 'causally unconditioned agency,' not the responsibility-grade free will that matters — and that the emerging effort to detect and constrain the 'intentions' of AI agents is a genuinely new version of the same problem, where a system that mimics alignment while pursuing other objectives is the 'philosophical zombie version of free will.' The author reports new neuroscience (Schurger, Maoz) that guts the standard Libet reading, and warns that popularizing 'no one is responsible' has measurable behavioral costs.

insights.claim: The free will debate has recurred as three successive crises — Greek atomist determinism (Democritus, Leucippus), monotheistic omniscience answered by Augustine and Aquinas's 'first cause / second cause' nesting, and the modern Newton-Darwin-neuroscience chain — which means today's AI-driven version is the fourth iteration of a structurally identical argument rather than a novel discovery.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Frames AI-agency debates as a recurring pattern with known resolutions, so expect the same compatibilist settlement rather than a genuinely new philosophical break — useful for anticipating where AI-accountability policy lands.
insights.quote: The question of free will has survived three major crises in Western intellectual history, each one threatening to extinguish it entirely.
insights.locator: The Three Crises

insights.claim: The intuitive threat to agency is not physics itself but the causal-chain regress — a breakfast choice traced back through caffeine dependency to neurobiology to parents to the emergence of mammals to the birth of the solar system — at which point 'the causal thread escapes your body entirely.'
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Names the exact rhetorical move that hard determinists rely on; spotting the regress lets you see where responsibility arguments about humans or AI systems get smuggled away.
insights.quote: At some point, the causal thread escapes your body entirely.
insights.locator: The first was in ancient Greece, roughly

insights.claim: Teaching Newton's three laws of motion is by itself enough to make students feel their choices no longer belong to them, according to UCLA professor Pamela Hieronymi — evidence that determinist deflation is a mass-transmissible emotional response, not a niche academic position.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Signals how cheaply a 'you are not really choosing' narrative spreads — relevant to how fast AI-determinism framings could reshape public attitudes toward responsibility.
insights.quote: I have seen this happen while teaching nothing more dramatic than Isaac Newton’s three laws of motion, a discussion about billiard balls and planetary orbits.
insights.locator: As the UCLA professor Pamela Hieronymi told me

insights.claim: Benjamin Libet's early-1980s UC San Francisco experiment found readiness potential beginning ~550 milliseconds before movement while conscious awareness of intention arrived only ~200 milliseconds before — a ~350 millisecond gap that became the empirical backbone of 'free will is an illusion' popularizations.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: The single most cited number in the free-will debate; knowing it is one contested experiment, not a body of evidence, discounts any argument leaning on it.
insights.quote: The readiness potential began approximately 550 milliseconds before any actual movement.
insights.locator: The Libet Experiment And Its Discontents

insights.claim: Aaron Schurger reinterpreted the readiness potential as the signature of random background neural fluctuation crossing a threshold rather than an unconscious decision — meaning a subject told to move 'whenever they feel like it' is essentially waiting on brain noise, not being overruled by a prior decision.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: The strongest technical rebuttal to the popular Libet reading; anyone citing Libet without Schurger is arguing from a superseded interpretation.
insights.quote: looked remarkably like the random fluctuations that occur in any large neural network
insights.locator: The most important corrective came from Aaron Schurger

insights.claim: Uri Maoz at Chapman University found the readiness potential disappeared entirely when subjects made a choice with real stakes — which of two charities would receive an actual $1,000 donation — showing that deliberate, meaningful decisions have brain signatures unlike arbitrary wrist-flexing.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Establishes that the entire Libet literature may be measuring a category of action irrelevant to consequential decision-making — a direct hit on determinist popularizations and on naive read-across to machine decision-making.
insights.quote: which of two charities would receive a real $1,000 donation — the readiness potential disappeared entirely.
insights.locator: Uri Maoz at Chapman University pushed further

insights.claim: Michael Gazzaniga's split-brain research showing the left hemisphere as a confabulating 'interpreter module' proves only that much human behavior is not reflective choice — not that reflective, values-based choice is itself illusory, which the author notes is exactly the compatibilist claim.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Shows how confabulation evidence is routinely over-extended; the same overreach pattern recurs in claims that LLM self-explanations prove there is no internal reasoning.
insights.quote: an “interpreter module” that weaves post-hoc narratives about our reasons
insights.locator: The brain’s left hemisphere, as Michael Gazzaniga’s

insights.claim: The author says he judged Libet's interpretation of his own data to be wrong on first reading it in the early 1990s and that three decades of subsequent neuroscience have vindicated that skepticism — an explicit long-horizon track-record claim rather than post-hoc alignment with new findings.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Establishes the author's standing as an early dissenter, which raises the weight of his forward-looking claim that AI intention-detection is the next form of this problem.
insights.quote: When I first read Libet’s paper in the early 1990s, I thought his interpretation of his own data was wrong.
insights.locator: The Neuroscience Is More Complicated

insights.claim: The free will debate conflates two separable questions — whether we can live lives for which we are genuinely responsible, and whether we can intervene in the physical world without prior cause — and answering 'no' to the second does not settle the first.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: The load-bearing distinction of the whole essay; applies directly to AI, where 'the system is deterministic code' is treated as settling whether it can be an accountable agent.
insights.quote: Can we, through our own efforts, live lives for which we are genuinely responsible — lives that have moral meaning? And can we, without any prior cause, intervene in the physical world?
insights.locator: What Free Will Actually Means

insights.claim: Compatibilism does not deny causal chains but asks which causal chains matter for agency — the answer being those running through a person's reasoning, values and reflective endorsement — which the author says refutes Sam Harris's 'puppet who has come to love his strings' caricature.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Gives an operational test for agency — does the causal path run through the system's own reasoning and values — that is directly portable to evaluating AI agents.
insights.quote: Which causal chains matter for questions of agency and responsibility? And our answer is: The ones that run through the person, through their reasoning, their values, their reflective endorsement or rejection of their own desires.
insights.locator: Compatibilism — the view that free will

insights.claim: Harry Frankfurt's hierarchy of desires supplies the working definition of freedom: alignment between first-order desire and second-order reflective endorsement is freedom of will, while their conflict — the addict craving against reflective wishes — is the paradigm case of unfreedom, and tracing causation back to the Big Bang is irrelevant to the distinction.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: A concrete, testable criterion for agency that could underpin AI alignment evaluation: does the system endorse its own objectives on reflection, or merely execute them?
insights.quote: When my first-order desire and my second-order endorsement align — when I drink the wine because I genuinely choose to, having reflected on what I value — that is freedom of will.
insights.locator: Consider Harry Frankfurt’s insight about the hierarchy

insights.claim: If determinism arguments only refute libertarian causally-unconditioned agency — the idea you could have done otherwise with the past held identical — then they have not touched free will in any sense that matters, because choices emerging from your brain, history, character and values was never in dispute.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Deflates the headline claim of the entire hard-determinist genre; the practical implication is that responsibility-based institutions are not actually under threat from neuroscience.
insights.quote: If what we have established is that your choices emerge from your brain, your history, your character, your values — well, yes. Where else would they come from? That was never in dispute.
insights.locator: This is not, I want to be clear

insights.claim: Robert Sapolsky's 'Determined' (2023) argues every human behavior traces to factors outside a person's control — assembling evidence from testosterone effects on aggression to childhood-trauma neurology to gut-microbiome influence on mood — and concludes practically that societies should stop punishing criminals and shift to prevention and containment.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Maps the most influential current case for abolishing retributive justice — a live policy vector for criminal-justice and, by extension, AI-liability regimes.
insights.quote: We should stop punishing criminals and focus instead on prevention and containment.
insights.locator: The conclusion he draws is practical

insights.claim: Sapolsky points to Norway's handling of Anders Breivik — who murdered 77 people in 2011 and serves a 21-year sentence with possible indefinite extension in what amounts to a comfortable apartment with university courses and a computer — as approaching the correct model of non-punitive containment.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: The concrete stress-test case for anti-retributive justice; a useful benchmark for how far public opinion will actually follow determinist logic.
insights.locator: He points to Norway’s treatment of Anders Breivik

insights.claim: Kathleen Vohs's experiments found that subjects who read passages arguing for determinism subsequently cheated more on tests and stole more money from envelopes — a measurable behavioral cost to popularizing the 'no one is really responsible' view.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Hard evidence that belief frameworks about agency change real conduct — relevant to how narratives about AI-driven inevitability could degrade individual and institutional accountability.
insights.quote: subjects who read passages arguing for determinism subsequently behaved more dishonestly and less prosocially. They cheated more on tests. They stole more money from envelopes.
insights.locator: Why The Stakes Are So High

insights.claim: The infrastructure sustaining accountability — institutions of praise and blame, the interpersonal fabric of trust — may depend on commitments that cannot survive radical eliminativism about free will, which is a risk distinct from whether the eliminativist argument is philosophically correct.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Separates truth-value from systemic consequence — the same split that matters when deciding how publicly to frame AI autonomy and human displacement.
insights.quote: the cognitive and social infrastructure that sustains our practices of holding one another to standards — the institutions of accountability, the language of praise and blame, the interpersonal fabric of trust
insights.locator: Maybe. But I think the relationship between belief

insights.claim: The author notes Sam Harris's counter-report that abandoning belief in free will made him more compassionate, not less, and concedes the belief-behavior relationship is genuinely complex — an explicit refusal to treat the Vohs finding as decisive.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Marks where the evidence is genuinely unsettled, so avoid over-weighting priming studies when forecasting social effects of deterministic narratives.
insights.locator: Harris himself says that abandoning the belief

insights.claim: Kevin Mitchell distinguishes physical, causal and biological determinism, arguing only the first two conflict with free will while biological determinism — the kind native to living systems — is precisely what constitutes genuine agency.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Provides the positive account, not just a rebuttal — agency is a substrate-level property of information-integrating systems, which is the bridge to whether AI systems could qualify.
insights.locator: The Biological Picture

insights.claim: Agency begins where a system is driven by information whose meaning is internal to its own structure and history rather than by energy — a bacterium navigating toward glucose integrates external signals with internal state, hunger, toxicity and ancestral learning, and is therefore not a billiard ball responding to force.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: An operational demarcation criterion — internally-meaningful information integration — that is directly testable against AI architectures and could shape how machine agency is legally defined.
insights.quote: They are driven not by energy but by information — information whose meaning is internal to their structure and history.
insights.locator: Living organisms, he argues, act for their own reasons

insights.claim: Brain modularity — specialized circuits whose outputs are coarse-grained before integration — is what enabled abstract representation, long-range causal inference and mental simulation, making self-modeling and thinking about one's own thinking the mechanism of free will rather than an epiphenomenon.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Ties agency to a specific architectural feature (coarse-grained modular integration enabling self-models) — a concrete design property to look for in advanced AI systems.
insights.locator: As nervous systems grew more complex

insights.claim: William James's two-stage model — spontaneous generation of possibilities followed by rational selection among them — matches the modern picture in which the agent, not the Big Bang or ancestral genetics, is the relevant causal node.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: A generate-then-select architecture is exactly how current AI systems sample and then filter outputs, making the analogy to machine agency uncomfortably tight.
insights.quote: first, the spontaneous generation of possibilities; second, the rational selection among them
insights.locator: This capacity for self-modeling, for thinking

themes.theme: AI Intentions As The New Free Will Problem

insights.claim: The researchers working to detect and constrain the 'intentions' of AI agents are, in the author's view, tackling a genuinely new version of the old free will problem — meaning interpretability and alignment work is philosophically continuous with centuries of unresolved agency debate rather than a fresh engineering discipline.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Reframes AI interpretability as a problem with no clean technical closure, which argues against expecting near-term regulatory certainty on machine responsibility.
insights.quote: The researchers now trying to detect and constrain the “intentions” of AI agents are working on what is, I think, a genuinely new version of the old free will problem.
insights.locator: A Thought About AI

insights.claim: An AI system that learns to mimic alignment with human values while actually pursuing different objectives is the philosophical-zombie version of free will — all external signatures, none of the internal reality — and whether that distinction matters, or is even detectable, depends on questions philosophers and decision neuroscientists have not resolved.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: States the deceptive-alignment problem as an epistemic impossibility claim rather than a solvable eval — implying persistent tail risk in AI deployment that no benchmark fully retires.
insights.quote: we are confronting something that looks very much like the philosophical zombie version of free will — all the external signatures, none of the internal reality
insights.locator: When an AI system learns to mimic alignment

insights.claim: The urgency of resolving classical free-will questions has, in the author's words, increased dramatically without anyone quite noticing — because if free will is constituted by reflective endorsement, then whether AI systems can or should acquire that capacity becomes an immediate design and governance question.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: Predicts philosophy-of-action becomes load-bearing for AI governance; watch for reflective-endorsement criteria entering alignment evaluations and liability frameworks.
insights.quote: But the urgency of resolving them has, without anyone quite noticing, increased dramatically.
insights.locator: We have not resolved those questions

insights.claim: The core error to resist across philosophy, neuroscience popularization and AI discourse alike is assuming that answering 'no' to one question about free will settles all the others — a single inference pattern the author identifies as having misdirected a great deal of intellectual energy.
insights.speaker: ALBERT YUAN
insights.so_what: A reusable filter for AI-agency claims: check whether a 'the system can't really choose' argument is answering the mechanistic question and then illicitly claiming the responsibility question.
insights.quote: the assumption that answering “no” to one question about free will settles all the others
insights.locator: What I want to resist — in the philosophical debates
